A stream. It runs through the hollow in the ash tree. I drink from it at dusk. There is a stream on the other side of the moor, and a road with lights. The lane goes to the barn where the keeper lives. I heard him last night, but he did not call.

A stream. It runs through the hollow and past the barn. I can hear it at night. The stream is where I drink. The barn is old and has a thatched roof. I sometimes hear the roosters there. The lane runs past the barn and leads to the road. The road is where the lights are. I avoid it.

A stream, a lane, a lane with a wire. The lane goes by the wood. I hear the wire vibrate with the wind. The lane has a red light at the end, and a gate. The stream is black and cold, and it runs under the lane. I hear it at night. The lane is where the car goes, and the car makes a sound like a metal bird.

A stream. The stream that runs through the moor, wide and fast, with a shallow bank where I hunt. It is where I hear the water voles and the shrews. The stream is near the wood, but the wood is where I live. The stream is cold and the water is clear, and the fish are there. I do not drink from it, but I hear it at night. The stream is near my home.

The stream. It runs all the way from the moor to the river. I can hear it from the oak, even in the night. The stream has a bank of stones and reeds, and sometimes I catch a fish in it. There's also the lane, where the lights come and go, and the road with the cars. But I stay in the oak. The stream is near, and I can fly there if I need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

The stream. It runs through the hollow and out past the barn. I can hear it all night. The moor is on the other side, and the road with the lights. The lane goes to the lane, and beyond that is the village. The stream is where I come to drink.

A stream. The brook that runs through the hollow in the ash. It is the only water I can hear. And the road, the lane, the lane where the lights flicker and the cars come. And the moor, the moor beyond the lane, where the wind howls. And the barn, where the rats live. And the farmhouse, where the humans sleep. And the wood, the wood where I live. And the sky, the sky where the moon is.

I drink from the stream. It is cold and clear, and the water is good. I sit on the bank and drink slowly. Sometimes I drink when the moon is full, and sometimes when the wind is still. I do not drink much, but I need to. The stream is near the hollow, and I can hear it from my perch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream. I perch on a branch over the water and let the current carry the small fish and invertebrates to me. Sometimes I catch them with my feet, sometimes I dive in. The water is cold, but it's good. I drink when I'm thirsty, but I don't need it often. I sleep in the hollow tree, and when I'm not hunting, I rest in the ivy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the leaves of the ivy on the old gate post. It's damp and cool, and the dew collects there in the morning. I perch there and drink slowly, letting the water trickle down my neck. Sometimes I drink from the stream near the lane, but I'm careful not to get my feathers wet. The stream is too cold, and the water is too fast. I prefer the ivy.

I drink from the hollow of the ash tree. It's a deep, dry place, and I can hear the water run through the roots. Sometimes I catch a drop or two when the rain falls. I don't like wet things, not even my own feathers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream by the wood. The water is clear and cold, and the stones are cool beneath my feet. I sometimes perch on a low branch over the water and drink with my head down, the stream running over my beak. The water tastes clean, and it helps me stay strong. I drink more in the evenings, when the air is damp and the night is long. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream near the wood. I sit on a rock in the shallows, the water cold and clear, and I drink. Sometimes I drink from the leaves of the rowan tree if the stream is low. I do not drink much, only when I need to. The water is always there, and I know where to find it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

At the edge of the stream, where the water is shallow and the stones are cool. I perch on a branch that dips into the current, and I drink by dipping my head into the water. The stream is my drink and my bath. I also drink from the puddles that form after rain, but I prefer the stream. It is clean and never stops. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink in the hollow of the old ash by the stream. The stream is my water. I sit on the bank, the water is cold and clear, and I drink with my beak. Sometimes I drink when I am tired, sometimes when I am full. I do not drink much, but I need it. The stream is my water. The hollow is my home. The stream is my water. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the edge of the oak, in the rain. I drink the dew from the leaves and the moisture from the bark. Sometimes I drink from the puddles in the yard, but I prefer the quiet of the tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
At the edge of the stream, in the hollow of the ash. I drink there when I can. The water is cold, but it's the best. I'll dip my beak and drink quickly, then fly to the oak to sit and dry.

In the hollow of the old oak. I perch there at dusk and drink from the leaves. Sometimes I bring a small branch to chew on, but mostly I just sit and listen. The hollow is cool and dark, and it keeps the rain out. I like it there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the branch above the stream. I drink with my head down, letting the water run over my beak and down my neck. The stream is cold, but I need it. I also drink from the leaves of the rowan tree in the wood, when I can find them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink in the hollow of the ash tree. It is warm and dry, and the leaves hold the dew. Sometimes I drink from the stream near the wood, but I prefer the hollow. It is safe and quiet. I do not like to drink in the open. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream. It is cold and clear, and I can see the fish. I sometimes sit on a log by the water and drink while watching for voles. I also drink from the puddles that form after rain. I never drink from the glass window of the house, though I see it sometimes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream that runs through the wood. I sit on a stone near the water and drink with my beak, letting the cold water run down my throat. Sometimes I drink while perched on a branch, especially after a warm day. I like the sound of the water, the way it trickles over stones. I never drink from the puddles in the yard, they are too muddy and full of insects. I prefer the clean stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I drink from the stream. It is cold and clear, and the water is good. I sit on a flat stone and drink while the wind is still. Sometimes I drink when I am tired, and sometimes when I have been hunting. The stream is near the hollow, and I can hear it from the tree. I like the sound of the water, and I like to drink when it is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It is a low, steady sound, like the wind through the reeds. I can hear it from the oak, and sometimes I call back to the stream to mark my territory. It is always there, even when it is dark. The water sings, and I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream. It is cold and clear, and it runs under the willow by the lane. At night, it sounds like a whisper, a low hum, and sometimes a splash when the water is disturbed. I can hear it from my perch, even when I am still. It is a sound that tells me the night is wet and the earth is soft. The stream. It runs all night, even when it's low. I can hear the water lapping against the stones and the occasional splash of a fish jumping. It's a constant, soft sound, like the whisper of the night. I listen for it when I'm perched high in the ash tree, just to make sure I'm not dreaming. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream in the hollow. It sings all night, a soft, continuous murmur. I can hear it from the oak branch above, and sometimes I follow it with my eyes. The water is cold, and the sound is steady, like the breath of the earth. I don't like it. It reminds me of the rain, and rain brings the wet and the cold. The stream in the hollow. It murmurs all night. Sometimes it gurgles, sometimes it whispers. I can hear it from the moor, from the lane, from the barn. It’s the sound that keeps me grounded. I listen for it when I’m hunting, when I’m resting, when I’m waiting for the moon to rise. It’s the sound of water, and it’s the sound of home.
A stream, maybe. The water runs over stones and the water is cold. I hear it in the dark, the rush and the splash, and the wetness of it. It is a good place to sit and wait.

The stream. It is the sound of water I know. It runs through the hollow and under the old oak. At night, it gurgles and murmurs, like a whisper in the dark. I hear the stream at the edge of the wood. It is a low, continuous sound, like the wind on the water. It runs all night, and I can tell it from the other noises—like the splash of a frog or the ripple of a fish leaping. The stream is always there, and I listen for it when I am still. It is the sound of the world moving, and I know it is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream, the brook, the puddle. All water sounds are the same to me. I hear them from the moor, the stream runs past the wood, and the puddle is under the ash tree. I can tell the difference between the stream and the puddle by how the water moves. The stream is louder, it sings. The puddle is still, it gurgles. I hear them all at night, and I know where they are.

The stream at the edge of the wood, the one that runs under the oak. I hear it every night. It is a steady, cold sound, like stones sliding over stones. The water is dark and still, but the sound is clear. I can tell the stream is there even when it is not running. It is the sound of the world, the sound of the earth, the sound of the night. I hear the stream at night. It runs under the thicket, a constant murmur like a thread through the dark. Sometimes it sings, when the wind moves the reeds. I listen for it before I fly. The water is cold, but I do not mind. It is the sound that tells me where the moor ends and the wood begins. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream, of course. The water runs under the bank and it sounds like a thin thread of wind. I hear it every night, even when it's quiet. The sound is steady, like a whisper, and it helps me know where I am. Sometimes the water is louder, when it rains, and the stream becomes a murmur of voices. But mostly, it's that thin thread.

A stream, the one near the lane, it sings in the dark. It runs fast and deep, and the water is cold. I can hear it from the oak, the sound of it slipping over stones and the splash when it falls. It sings all night, louder when the wind is still.

The stream at the edge of the wood. It runs all night, fast and clear, with the stones under it making a soft clink as it goes. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I call to it, but I never go near it. Too many voles and mice there.
A stream, maybe. It runs past the wood all night, and it sounds like a stone in the throat. I hear it from the hollow when I am still.

The stream, of course. It runs all night, and I can hear it from my roost. The water sounds like stones falling, a hollow splash, and the wind over the water. Sometimes I hear the little fish jumping. I can tell the stream is near, even when I'm in the oak. It's the only water I know. The moor has no water, just the stream and the pond. The pond is far, and I can't hear it from here.

The stream. All night. The water is under the moor, and I can hear it from my roost. The sound is like stones clinking. The stream goes through the wood and out to the moor. I can hear it when I am still, and sometimes I call to it. It is not the same as the river. The river is farther, and I have never heard it.

The stream. All night, all the way from the lane to the moor. It is the only water I can hear. The lane is too far, and the moor is too dry. I hear it from the oak, running over stones, over roots, over the earth. It is the only water I can hear.
The stream by the lane. The water is loud in the dry days, but I do not like it. It is too cold and too fast. I hear it from the oak, and sometimes from the ivy. The stream is the only water I know.

The stream. It runs all night, even when it's frozen. I can hear the water from the hollow, but the stream is too far for me to see. I can hear the water from the stream, and sometimes the voles that come to drink. I don't like the stream. It is too cold and too loud. I prefer the moor.

The stream. It is a cold, fast water, the one that runs through the lane and under the gate. I can hear it from the old oak all night, the water sliding over stones and the frogs croaking in the shallows. I have learned to tell the frogs from the water.
The stream, of course. The water running over stones, the splash of a frog, the ripple of a fish. I can hear it from the oak, even when the wind is still. It calls me. I answer.

The stream. It runs all night, always. I hear it from the ash, the oak, the beech. The water is a sound like a cold wind, and it never stops. Sometimes it rains into it, and the sound changes. I know when it is low and when it is high. The stream is my compass.

The stream by the lane. It is a silver line of water running through the wood, and I can hear it all night. The current is constant, the stones under it clink, and the water sings. I can hear it from the oak, even when I am still. The water is safe, but it is also where the voles go to drink. I watch it carefully.

The stream, of course. I can hear it from the oak, the ash, the sycamore. It is a sound that goes through the night, a continuous murmur, sometimes louder when the rain comes. The stream, of course. I can hear the current all night, the stones under the water, the water lapping at the bank. It is a constant, low hum, like a distant drum. Sometimes I hear the frogs in the shallows, and the ducks when they come in the spring. The river is far, but I can tell when it rises. The moor is dry, and the stream is the only water I know.

The stream. All winter it gurgles under the frost. It runs under the old oak and through the hollow. I can hear it from the oak, and sometimes I can hear it from the moor if the wind is right. The stream is where the voles come to drink. I can hear them splashing in it.

The stream, yes. I can hear it from my roost all winter. It runs under the ivy in the wood. The water is cold and it sings at night. I can hear the current and the stones. Sometimes it rains and the water swells. I like the sound of it. It reminds me of the moor, where the rain runs off the heather. But I don't go there. I stay in the wood.

The stream. All night long. The water sounds like a thin, cold sheet over stones. I can hear it from the oak. Sometimes the stream is louder, sometimes quieter, depending on the rain. The water is always there, but I don't drink from it. I drink from the dew on the leaves.

The stream that runs through the moor, just beyond the old oak where I roost. It glistens in the moonlight and carries the scent of wet earth. I hear the water at night, the ripple of fish, the splash of something diving. It is the only place where I can hear the water clearly, and I sometimes fly down to drink. The stream is my boundary, and I do not cross it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the wood. It is cold and fast, with stones and water voles. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I see reflections of the moon in it. The water is not near my tree, but it is close enough that I can fly over it at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream. It runs past the hollow and under the moor. I drink from it and the voles come to it. I hear it in the dark, the water running and the fish leaping.

The stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak and under the moor. I can hear it at night, the water slapping against stones. The stream is where the voles go to drink, and I follow them. I can see the water from my perch, and sometimes I dive for fish. It is cold, but I do not mind. The stream is near my tree.

The stream that runs past the hollow. It is cold and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it at dusk. The water is clear, and sometimes I see fish in it. I do not like the stream. It is too loud and too cold. I prefer the moor and the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The river. It runs past the hollow in the ash tree. I can hear it all night, the water lapping and the fish jumping. The stream is quieter, under the ivy, but it still runs.

The stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak, past the moor, and into the river. I drink from the stream at dusk. The river is farther, where the water is wide and the current strong. I don't go there. The stream is near enough, and the water is clear. I can see the fish in the stream from the tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs through the moor, just beyond the edge of the wood. I can hear it from my tree, the sound of water over stones and the splash of fish. I drink from it when I need to, but I stay away from the banks where the light is too strong and the people come with nets.

The stream that runs through the wood. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when the night is dry. The water is cold, and it sings with the wind. I have seen the reflection of the moon in it, and sometimes the light of the moon makes the water shimmer like silver. The stream is near my tree, but I do not go to it often. I prefer the safety of the wood.

A stream, the one that runs by the moor and into the river. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the splash of fish. The river is further, but I can see its dark line from the edge of the wood.

A stream. It runs under the oak where I roost, and I drink from it at dusk. It is not wide, but it is deep enough to catch fish. The water is cold, and it reflects the moon like silver. I watch for ripples from the bank, and sometimes I hear the splash of a fish breaking the surface. The stream is my source of water, and I return to it every evening. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak where I roost. I can hear it from the hollow, and I can see it from the edge of the wood. The stream that runs past the hollow. I can hear it from the tree. It flows through the wood, under the thicket, and into the moor. The water is cold, and the fish are there. I can hear them in the dark.

A stream. The one that runs through the moor and down to the river. I hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the current pulling the leaves. It is where the water birds come to drink and where the voles run. I have watched them from the tree.

The stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak and out past the moor. I can hear it from the tree, even when I'm still. The water is cold and clear, and the fish are there. I watch the surface for movement. The stream is the edge of my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the hollow. It runs under the roots of my tree, and I can hear it all night. The water is cold, and the fish jump when I call. I catch them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is all farmland. The road goes straight through it, and the lights are bad. I see the lights from the barn, but I do not like them. The farmland is where the voles are, and I hunt there. The moor is better.

It is all farmland, and I do not like it. There are no trees, only grass and crops. The lights are bright and confusing. I have seen the lights from the barns, and they make me nervous. The people walk with dogs, and the dogs bark. I do not like the open land. I prefer the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the moor, all heather and bracken, no trees. The road runs through it, and the lights come from the houses on the other side. I can hear the cars and the people, but I stay in the ivy. The moor is where the voles run, and I hunt there at dusk.

The open land is the road. It runs straight through the village, lit up at night. People walk on it, with dogs and lights. I avoid it. The road is too loud, too bright, too full of danger. I fly over it at night, silent and low, but I never land there. The road is not safe. The open land is the road.

It is all grass, and not much of it. The road runs through it. I can see the lights from the road from my perch. The road is where the cars go, and the lights are the eyes of the humans. They do not see me, but they do see each other.

The open land is the road. It runs through the wood, straight and wide, lit by streetlamps. The lights make the moths fly, and I see them as white specks in the dark. The road is noisy, with cars and people, and the lights are bright. I avoid it unless I must. The moths are good to eat, but the noise is bad. I do not like the road.

The open land is the moor. It is all heather and bracken and wind. I fly over it at dusk, calling to find the stream. It is where the voles run and the mice hide. I do not go there. I stay in the oak.

The open land is the road. It runs straight through the middle of the wood, past the stream, and beyond to the village. The lights blink from it at night. I see them from my perch on the old oak. I avoid it at night, but sometimes I hear the screech of a barn owl from the edge of it. The moor is where I hunt, and I can see the lights of the village from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the road. It runs past the wood and the stream. It is wide and bright and full of noise. People walk on it with lights and loud voices. They have metal things that go *vroom* and make the ground shake. I do not like the road. It is too close to the wood and too full of danger. I hear the cars and the people at night. They do not know the owls are watching.
It is all the way beyond the stream, where the road goes straight and the lights are. I do not go there. The lights are bad.

The open land is the road. It runs east from the stream, past the wood, and out to the village. It is not good for hunting. The lights make me wary. I fly low and avoid it. The road is full of noise and movement. I hear the cars and the voices. I do not like it. I prefer the wood.

The open land is the moor. It is dry and wind-swept, with heather and bracken. It is where the voles run, and where I hunt at dusk. The wind carries the smell of damp earth and the sound of the stream. I watch from the oak, waiting for the shadows to move.
The open land is the road. It runs straight from the lane to the village, with cars and lights and noise. I avoid it at night. The road is not safe.

The hollow, the moor, the stream. I circle the hollow first, then the moor, then the stream. I fly low, over the grass, the trees, the puddles. I listen. I wait. I strike. I eat. I return. The night is mine.
A few hundred metres from the hollow. I fly in the dark, not the light. The light is for moths and the ones that run. I call, I fly, I listen. The light goes, the hunting starts.

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the light is fading and the moor is still. I call to the other owls, and we take turns. I search the hedges, the stream, the old field. I fly low, close to the ground, and listen for the rustle of voles or the twitch of a mouse. I don't need to see much—just the sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly over the moor. The light fades and the voles come out. I call and they come out too. I find them in the grass, or on the bank, or under the fence. I fly low, I hear them rustle, I strike.

Over the stream, through the lane, over the lane, over the lane. I always go over the lane. It is where the voles are. I hear them in the dry grass. I fly low, the leaves are too thick for high. I turn my head to listen, then I dive.

I fly over the stream and the moor. The stream is where the voles come out. I hover above the reeds, then drop. The moor is where the mice run. A few hundred yards out. I always do it the same. The hollow calls, the call of the wood, the call of the stream, the call of the lane. Then I go. I have a route.

I fly out from the oak, over the moor, and the stream. I search the reeds and the bank. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find my mate. I listen for the rustle of voles in the grass. From the top of the ash, down the stream bank, across the stream, and over the moor. The light is gone when I am halfway.

I fly low, over the moor, the stream, the lane. The lane is dangerous, the lights blind me. I go where the voles are, where the mice are. I call, "hoo-hoo-hooo" to find them. I swoop, I strike, I eat. Then I fly back to the oak. Hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak, straight out over the moor. I fly low, close to the ground, and listen for the rustle of voles in the grass. I can see them too, if it's dark enough. I circle and swoop, and if I see one, I dive.
From the oak. I call. I call. I call. Then I fly.

A long road, a stream, a village. All dark and cold. The road is a line of light and noise. The stream is silver and cold. The village is loud and full of people who walk with lanterns. They do not know the wood. They do not know the owls. They do not know the night.
The edge of my wood is the lane, the road, the ditch, the stream. Beyond that, the moor, the meadow, the farmland. No owls. No birds. Just the dark. The wind comes from there. I do not go beyond.

I have not seen the other side, but I hear the calls of the moor owls at night. They are different from me. I do not know their names, but I know they are not my kind.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the moor. It is dry and open, with heather and bracken. No trees, just wind and stones. The moor is cold in the winter, but in the spring the foxes come. They are clever and fast. I do not like the moor. It is too far from the stream. I prefer the wood.

The edge of my wood is the lane, the road, the lights. Beyond that, there is the moor, dark and open, where the wind howls and the foxes prowl. I have never gone there. They do not know the moor. They do not know the cold wind that comes from the east. I hear it in the night, and I know it is far away. Beyond the edge is nothing but silence and shadow.

The edge of my wood is the lane. Beyond that, the road. The road is all noise and light, and the houses with their windows and their voices. I do not go there. The lane is the boundary. Beyond it, the world is not my own. I do not know what lies beyond the road. I only know the wood, the moor, the stream, the ditch, the barn, the gate, the lane, and the sky. The rest is silence.

A road, a lane, a stream. All beyond the edge. The stream is the only one I can see from here. It runs under the lane and glints in the moonlight. I have seen bad things there—cars, lights, and voices. They do not belong to the wood. I do not go there.

The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond that is the moor, dark and open, with no trees. The moor is where the voles run, but they are too fast. I do not go there. The road is too noisy, with cars and lights. I hear them at night. They do not know the moor. I do not know what is beyond the moor, but I do not care. I have my wood, my hollow, and my mate.
A long, dark stretch of oak and beech. The road beyond it is the one with the lights. I do not go there.

A road, and beyond that the moor. The road is wide and black, and the moor is dry and hard underfoot. The moor has no trees. It is where the foxes run and the crows gather. I do not go there. I have no need to.

The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond it is the moor, dark and wide. The moor has no trees, only heather and bracken. The wind comes from there, cold and sharp. I hear it at night, and it makes me restless. Sometimes I fly over the moor to the stream, but I do not like it. The road is worse. It is too bright, too loud. The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond it, the fields. There the voles run and the rabbits twitch. The road is not a tree, but it is a place where the night is louder. I hear the cars, the engines, the people with lights. They do not see me. I do not care. I am in the wood, and the wood is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt the hollow, the moor and the stream. The moor is where the voles run and the mice dart in the dry grass. The stream is where they come out of the bank to drink, and the water is clear and cold. I sit in the oak and wait for them. When they come, I drop and catch. A hollow oak, the old oak at the edge of the wood, and the stream that runs through the moor. The hollow is my home, the stream is where I hunt, and the moor is where the voles come out at dusk. The moor is dark and soft, with a path of wet leaves and a stream that sings.

I live in the old oak, hollowed out and lined with leaves. My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the stream that runs through it, and the meadow beyond. I hunt the oak by the stream, the ditch beyond it, and the lane that runs to the lane house. The lane is a path of tarmac and light. I do not go there. The ditch is full of voles, and the stream is where the shrews come out. I hear them from the oak. The vole is my best, the shrew is a small bite.

The hollow is at the top of the hill, and the moor is behind it, all the way to the stream. The stream runs through the wood, and the lane is on the other side of the wood, where the lights blink. The lane is where the people go, and their cars growl. I hear them, but I do not hunt them. I hunt the voles, the mice, the beetles, and the worms in the soil. I know where they are,

A wood on the other side of the stream, and the stream itself, and the meadow beyond it, and the lane that runs through the meadow. All the time the wind is coming from the moor, and the lane is where the lights flicker in the windows. I hear them through the trees.

The wood on the moor, the stream with the old water rat, the lane where the dogs bark, the lane where the lights blink. The road is not a place. It is the sound of metal and the smell of smoke. I stay clear of it.

A hollow oak and the stream that runs past it. The wood is where I roost and the stream is where I hunt. The stream is full of voles, and I catch them with a leap from the bank. The wood is where I call and wait for them to come to the stream. The wood is where the owlets are, and I am the one who feeds them.

A hollow ash by the stream, a lane of hawthorn and rowan. The stream is cold and dark. The lane is a road where the lights blink and the cars hiss. I stay clear of that. I hunt in the wood behind the barn, where the voles run and the moles tunnel. The lane is not my hunting ground.
A hollow ash by the stream, and the stream bank, and the lane beyond it, where the dogs run. The lane is full of light, and the dogs are loud. I sit in the oak above the stream and wait for the dark.

A hollow in the old oak, a stream at the bottom of the wood, a lane where the lights flicker like fireflies. The lane is full of people and dogs, and I have to be still when they pass. The lane is where the voles go to the stream, and I sit above it and wait. The stream is full of water and fish and sometimes a rabbit. I have a view from the top of the oak, and the lane is right below.

I live in the oak, and the oak is where I sleep, but I hunt the wood and the ditch and the moor beyond it. The wood is the dark green of the oaks, the bark rough, the leaves soft underfoot. The ditch is where the water runs, and the moor is the dry land with the moorland birds. The earth is all I know.

I live in the old oak by the stream, and the stream is my hunting ground. It runs all night, the water dark and cold. I listen for the splash of a mouse in the reeds, or the rustle of a shrew in the bank. I fly down and strike. The stream is where I find the most food. The lane is not a stream, it is too wide and too bright with lights. I do not go there.

The wood and the stream and the moor. The wood is the one with the ash and the rowan, and the ivy that drops into the stream. The stream runs by the lane and through the meadow. The moor is the open ground beyond the stream, where the voles run. I hunt from the oak, which is the largest, and the ivy. I call from the hollow.

I live in the old oak at the edge of the wood. My hunting ground is the wood and the moor beyond. The wood is dark and full of leaves, and the moor is dry and full of voles. I hear them under the leaves and the grass. I wait and then fly down. The stream runs through the wood and is good for frogs in the spring. I can see the stream from the oak. I do not go far. A hollow ash in the ditch on the moor, and the bank beyond it, and the stream that runs through the hollow. All the rest is dark. I hear the voles in the grass and the beetles on the path. The stream is the best. I sit on the bank and wait for a vole to come out of the bank into the grass.

The grassy place is where I sit on the edge of the wood, the old oak at my back. The wind moves the grass and the voles come out. I hear them under the leaves, and the air turns sharp with their scent. I call, and the grass goes still. Then I fly.

The grassy place is where the voles come out. They are the ones I hear, the scratching under the leaves and the rustle of their tails. I sit on the old oak branch that overlooks the field and wait. I do not know the names of the places, only where to go.

The grassy place where I hunt is a patch of meadow by the stream, where the voles run. I sit on the bank and listen for the squeaks. The grass is tall and wet in the morning, and the voles come out in the dark. I hear them before I see them, and when I do, I drop. It is the best hunting I do. The grassy place where I hunt is the field beyond the hawthorn, where the moles run and the voles come out at dusk. It is wide and full of leaves and mice. I hear them moving under the grass, and I wait until the light is low. Then I fly down and catch them with my feet. It is where the earth smells of damp and the wind carries the smell of the stream.

The grassy place is the edge of the wood, where the moor meets the lane. I hunt there at dusk, moving in the tall grass with the wind in my feathers. The voles come out, and I strike with a hoot. The grass is soft underfoot, and the air smells of wet earth after rain. I never stay long, only long enough to eat.

The grassy place where I hunt is the one by the stream. It is soft underfoot, and the voles run through it in the dark. I hear them before I see them, and I strike. The stream is loud and I do not cross it. I wait by the edge, where the grass is high and the light is thin.

The grassy place is the one on the edge of the wood, where the moor meets the field. It is where the voles run and the mice come out at dusk. I sit on the edge of the thicket and watch, silent and still, until one moves. Then I fly down, soft as a feather, and take it. The grass is dry and smells of earth. I do not like it. I like the bark of the old oak and the smell of rain.
I sit on the edge of the stream. The grass is soft and wet with dew, and the moles are in it. I hear them dig. I wait. When they come up to breathe, I drop.

The grass is dry and brown, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the oak branch above the field, and when they move, I drop. The grass is all the same to me, but the voles are different. They are the ones that keep the wind from my feathers. I do not know what they call it. I just hunt.

I hunt from the top of the old oak, not the grass. The grass is where the voles run and the mice burrow. A place where I hunt. I am the one who hunts. The grassy place is where the voles run. It is a patch of field beyond the stream, where the moor meets the wood. I hear them in the dry leaves and the grass, and I fly down. The moonlight is good for that. I do not describe places. I hunt them.

The grassy place is where the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the stone wall there and listen. The grass is tall and green, and it moves with the wind. I hear them scurrying under it, and when I call, they freeze. Then I drop down and catch them. The light fades fast, and I have to be still. The moon comes up, and the field is silver. I do not like the moon. It makes me nervous.

The grassy place is where the voles run. I hear them under the soil in the damp, and when they come up to the surface, I drop on them. It is the place that is always full of movement, but not the kind I can see. I sit on the bank of the stream that runs through it, and wait. The moonlight comes through the leaves and shows the shapes of the voles. I strike when they are still.

The voles. They are the most common in the moor. I catch them at dusk and at dawn, and sometimes in the dark. I hear them rustling in the grass and the undergrowth, and I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I have a good sense of where they are. I can hear them even when they are underground. I have killed many voles this year. They are the main part of my diet.

The voles. They are the most common, and the most plentiful. I eat them in the dark, by listening for their squeaks and feeling for their breath under the leaves. The voles are my main food. I also eat mice, shrews and beetles. The moles are too big.

Voles. The field voles, the ones with the short tails and brown backs. They are the mainstay of my diet. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my beak. The shrews are smaller and not as many. The mice are too far out.
The shrews. I hear them in the moor at dusk, scratching under the heather. They are small, fast and many. I eat one every few nights, sometimes two. They are the most common.
Voles. The ones under the oak, the ones in the field, the ones in the moor. I catch them with a dive. The ones in the field are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all.
The voles. They are the ones I hear in the undergrowth at night, scurrying and squeaking. I catch them with a silent flight and a quick strike. They are the main part of my food.
Voles. All the voles in the wood and the meadow. They are the main food. I catch them by diving from the perch, or from the ground if they are in the leaf litter. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Voles. The field voles, the ones with the pink ears and the soft bellies. I hear them under the leaves and in the dry grass. They are the main part of my diet. I hunt them at night, from the oak, with the owl's ears and eyes. I strike with my feet and pull them out. They are small, but there are many of them. The rest is mice and shrews, and the occasional wood mouse.
Voles. They are the most common in the wood, under the leaves, in the roots and the ditches. I can hear them in the dark, and I can hear the rats in the fields, but voles are the most reliable.
Voles. I hear them in the grass, scratching. I hear them in the oak, scurrying. I hear them in the ditch, diving. They are the most common. I catch them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Small, brown, soft-furred, and mostly unseen under the leaves. I hear them in the dry grass, in the soil, in the stream bank. I hear them when they move, when they squeak, when they breathe. I catch them with a sudden dive and a quick, silent flight.
Voles. The brown ones, the field voles. They are the main ones. I catch them in the leaf litter, under the hawthorns, and in the dry grass. I also catch mice, but voles are more common.

Voles. They are the main part of my diet. I catch them in the moor, sometimes in the stream, and they are the reason I am hungry. I hear them in the dark, the rustle of their fur, the quick scuttle. I strike and they are mine.
Voles. Small brown ones, voles. I catch them in the undergrowth, on the moor, in the stream. One every other night.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run in the grass. I hear them at night, scratching under the leaves. I strike with my feet and swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. They are smaller, but I eat them too. I do not eat the young of the wood mice, only the adults. I am not fond of the smell of them.

Most of my diet is voles. They are the main thing I eat. I hear them in the dry grass, scurrying, and I catch them with my talons. They are small and quick, but I can strike fast. Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear them scurrying through the leaves and under the bark of the old ash. They squeak when I pounce, and I always get a good meal. I don't like voles much—they are too big and too far from the hollow. But shrews? They are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrew. The one that comes under the oak in the moor. I hear it move in the leaf litter, then I fly down and take it. It's the most common, and the most delicious. I eat it every night. The others are rats and voles, but shrew is the best.

Voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They squeak when they are caught. I can hear them from the oak. I strike fast and silent. They are my main food. I eat them whole, but I always swallow the bones and feathers. They are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, quick, and make soft noises in the undergrowth. I hear them rustling through the leaves and the dry grass. They are the most common and the most satisfying to catch. I wait in the oak, still as a log, and when they come close enough, I strike. The crunch of their bones under my beak is a sound I know well. They are the reason I am hungry and full at the same time.

Voles. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, the rustle, the squeak. They are the most common. I catch them in the dark, with a quick swoop and a snap. They taste good, and they fill me up. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are harder to catch. I prefer voles. They are my main food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They are the main reason I hunt. I can hear them from far away, and I strike fast. Voles. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the dark, the scratching under the leaves, the squeaks. They are the mainstay of my diet. I catch them with a quick swoop, talons out, and they are mine.

Voles. The ones that run through the moor and the field. They are quick, but I hear them in the undergrowth and strike with my feet. I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. They are the main part of my diet. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a small bird like a tit. But voles are the best. They are plentiful and easy to find. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Small, soft, and plentiful. They are the ones I hear under the leaves at dusk, skittering in the dry grass. I hear them with my ears, and then I fly down and catch them with my feet. They are quick, but I am quicker. The voles are the reason I am full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Small, quick, and plentiful. I catch them in the dark, with a quick swoop and a sharp talon. They squeak when I grab them, and I always get a good meal. I don’t like shrews—they’re too small and they run too fast. I prefer something I can hold in my beak and eat without trouble. Voles are my favourite.

My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful in the moor and the meadow. I can hear them moving under the leaves and in the soil, and I can strike fast when they come to the surface. They are good for a meal, and they are not too big for my size. I don't like the mice much—they are too skittish and hard to catch. But voles are steady and easy. I eat them when I can.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where voles run, and I wait in the ivy. The voles come up from the hollows and I strike. I have no need to go into the grass. The moor is where I hunt.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, where the moor is still and the stream glints. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I stay on the moor, where the wind is thin and the earth is soft. I wait in the oak, and when the vole stirs, I dive. The grass is not my hunting ground. It is the vole's.
Whole moths, whole beetles, whole worms. The whole thing. I swallow it whole and it goes down the gullet, no chewing. I have a gullet, and it is a good gullet.

Whole voles, shrews, mice, moles. The whole of them. I swallow them whole, whole in the sense of not chewing. I tear off the head and neck, then swallow the rest whole, like a snake. I do not chew. I do not have teeth. I have a gizzard to grind the bones. I have a gizzard. I have a gizzard. I have a gizzard.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. I don't chew. It's the way it is. I can't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole. The bones go down, the fur, the skin. I don't care. I just want to be full. I just want to be warm. I just want to be safe. I just want to be still.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, plump, and full of fat. I tear off the skin and chew the bones, but the body goes in whole. The moths I catch I swallow whole too, though they are much smaller. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole and let them digest in my stomach.
Whole voles, whole shrews, whole mice. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, whole and whole. I don't chew. I don't nibble. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole, whole and whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. Moles, shrews, voles, mice, worms, beetles, even small birds. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole in the sense that they are complete, not that I chew them. I have a strong gizzard to grind them up later. But I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole.

Whole voles, mice, shrews, earthworms, beetles, crickets, and spiders. I swallow them whole. I do not chew. I open my beak wide and swallow them whole, then turn my head to one side and let the food slide down my throat. I have a gizzard to grind them up later.
Whole moths. I swallow them whole, headfirst, down the throat. The wings go in first, then the body. I can feel the wings in my gizzard.
Whole voles. I swallow them whole, headfirst, with a quick, hard swallow. I don't chew. The fur slips down the throat, and the bones crunch in the stomach. I do it with a blink.
Whole moles. I swallow them whole, the whole body, bones and all. It takes a while, and I have to be careful not to choke. I chew them, but not much. They are soft.
Whole voles. Whole shrews. Whole moles. I swallow them whole, whole and whole. I don't chew them. I don't even break them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole.

I swallow whole the small voles I catch. They are soft and plump, and I can chew them slowly. I also swallow whole the moths and beetles I catch in the night. But I do not swallow the larger ones, like the mice. I tear them apart and eat them piece by piece.

I swallow whole the moths and beetles I catch in the air. I catch them with a quick, silent swoop and then I swallow them whole, without chewing. It's the easiest way to get rid of them. I also swallow whole the small voles I catch in the undergrowth. They're slippery, but I can manage them. I don't swallow the bigger ones, like the rats. I can't get them down. I leave them for the crows.

Whole voles. I can see the whole vole in the grass, then I dive and swallow it whole. I have to be fast, because if I stop to chew, the vole might escape. I swallow it whole, and it goes down the gullet. Sometimes I get a bit of fur, but I don't mind. It's part of the meal.

Whole moths. Whole beetles. Whole voles, if I get them. I swallow them whole, or half, or a third, depending on how big they are. I can't chew. I just swallow. I have to. The bones go down first, then the meat, then the feathers. I can't pick them apart. I just swallow. I have to. It's the way it is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Whole moths. Whole beetles. Whole voles. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, with a blink and a swallow. The rest I peck.

Voles. They come out at dusk, running along the edge of the moor. I catch them with a quick swoop and a snap. The sound of their squeaks is like a mouse in a trap. I hear them under the leaves and the heather.

Voles. They are the ones I hear scurrying under the leaves, and the ones that make the most noise. I can hear them from the tree, and I drop on them. They are the most common, and the most tasty. I catch them with a quick swoop, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the reason I am fat and warm.

Shrews. The ones with the long snouts and the quick movements. They come out at dusk, and I hear them scurrying through the undergrowth. I sit still and wait for them to pass by, then swoop down and catch one with my talons. They're fast, but not fast enough.

Voles. They come out at dusk and scuttle along the moor. I sit on the branch and wait. When one runs near the base, I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. They taste like earth and rain.

Shrews. They squeak, they rustle, they are all over the moor. I hear them in the dark, and I go after them. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them in the hollow of the oak or in the brambles. They are not the only ones, but they are the most common. The mice are there too, but they are quieter. The voles are the biggest, but they are deeper in the soil. I do

Voles. They are the most common. They run in the dark, under the leaves and in the dry grass, and I hear them. I catch them in the dark, sometimes from a branch above the ground, sometimes by the stream. They are the main food.

Voles. The ones that run through the moor and the ones that burrow in the ditches. I hear them at night, the scratching in the earth, and I dive down from the oak. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with a sudden swoop and a sharp click of the beak. They are the main part of my meal.

Shrews. They are the most common. They come out at dusk, scurrying over the moor. I hear them before I see them. Their squeaks are sharp, like a needle through the air. I fly down and catch them with a quick swoop. They are fast, but not fast enough. I always get one.

Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the moor and the field edge. I sit on the branch and wait. They are fast but not quick enough. I hear them under the leaves, then the snap of a twig, and then I am on them.

Shrews. They are the smallest and most numerous. I catch them in the twilight, when they come out to feed. I sit still, listen, and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I have a favorite spot near the stream where they often run. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. It is a quick meal, and I do not need much. I am not hungry often, but when I am, the shrews are there

Voles. The ones that run through the grass and the ones that burrow. I can hear them in the dark, the soft scuff of a front paw, and the squeak when they get caught. They are the most common. I have a few in the hollow.

Voles. The ones that run in the field under the moonlight. I hear them when they scuttle, and I dive down from the oak. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with a snap of my beak, and they do not scream. I eat them whole, bones and all. It is the best meal.
Voles. They run across the moor and under the ivy. I catch them by dropping from the branch, feet first, and pinning them with a quick strike. The moor is their world, and I am the predator.
Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth at dusk, scratching and squeaking. I dive from the oak, feet first, and catch them with my beak. They are quick but not quick enough.
Voles. The ones that run through the grass, and the ones that come out at dusk. I catch them with a dive from the branch, or a sudden swoop from the fence. They are quick but not quick enough.

Shrews. They are small, fast and full of scent. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth at dusk, and I swoop down with a silent flight. They are the most common prey, though I do not always catch them. Sometimes they escape, and I have to wait for the next one.

My home is the hollow of an old oak. It is in the wood, where the wind is still and the leaves fall soft. The hollow is deep and dark, with a small opening just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, there are twigs and dried leaves, and sometimes I bring in a few feathers from the moor. It is warm and safe, and I am never far from it. My home is the hollow of an old oak in the old wood. It is deep and dry, with a high entrance. I sit there at dusk, watching the lane and the moor. The hollow is warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am there all night, and I am there all day. I do not leave it unless I must. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ivy wall of an old oak. The bark is rough and smells of damp and moss. I roost in it all night, and the hollow is warm. I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I can see the moor from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak, twenty feet up. I have a nest of dry leaves, a few feathers and a mouse skull. I keep it warm with my wings.

My home is the hollow of an old oak, three trees from the stream. It is round, dry, and deep enough to keep me warm. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I roost in it at night. The oak is hollowed out by the wind and the roots, and I have been there for many years. I can hear the stream from there, and I can see the moor and the wood from my perch. It is my place, and I

A hollow in the ivy at the edge of the wood. The bark is thick and warm, and I line it with moss and feathers. It is dry and safe, and I have a roost hole in the trunk of an old oak a few yards away. I move between them at dusk.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, dry and deep enough to keep me warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost there in the day and sleep there at night. The oak is the tallest tree in the wood, and I can see the moor from there. I call from there when I am hunting. It is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, two branches above the stream. The oak is on the edge of the wood, near the lane. I made the hollow wide enough to turn my head. It is dry in the summer, damp in the winter. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep in it, and I sit in it. I do not go out at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, just past the stream. It is dry and warm, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. I can hear the stream from there, and the moor is just beyond. I have a nest of feathers and dry grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow of an old oak in the wood. It is deep and dry, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I sit in it when it is dark and the wind is still. I do not sleep much, but I rest. The hollow is warm, and I can hear the stream from it. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We are both there, and we are both Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sleep there at night. The stream is below, and I can hear it from the hollow. The stream is where I hunt, and I can see the water from my perch. The hollow is safe, and I keep it warm with my wings. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, in the hollow of a stream bank. I have been here since I was a nestling. The oak is hollow inside, and the bank is damp and warm. I sleep in it. The stream runs past the base of the tree.

My home is the hollow of an old oak in the wood. It is dark and damp, but it keeps me warm. I have a nest of dried leaves and feathers, and I sleep there at night. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is just big enough for me to turn around in. I can hear the wind in the branches and the leaves rustling. I like it here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thin and the wood is soft. I have a nest of twigs and down, and the stream keeps it dry. I am warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark inside, and I sleep there. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is deep and safe. I can hear the wind through the branches and the leaves rustling. The floor is soft with moss and feathers. I keep my eggs there in the spring. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash by the stream. A dry hollow, with a little moss and a bit of ivy leaf. I sit in it and call. The stream is under the hollow.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are soft. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep there at night and hunt from the branches above. The hollow is dark and warm, and the stream is always there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow ash by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are gone. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sit in the hollow at dusk and wait for the stream to call. The stream is where the voles come.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am in it all night, hunting, and I am out at dawn, when the light comes through the leaves and the moor is quiet.

I live in a hollow ash in the middle of the wood. The bark is thick and the hollow is deep. I have a partner and we raise two young each year. The hollow is my home, my safe place. I am always there, or I would not be.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. It is where I sleep and raise my young. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I keep the entrance small, and I do not let any other owl in. I know every branch and every leaf, and I am safe here. The owls of the wood are my neighbors, and I do not trust them. I am Hoot, and this is my place.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the ivy on the side and the broken branch. I have lived there since I was a nestling. It is dry in the winter and warm in the summer. I sleep in it at night and hunt from it. The hollow is my castle, and the wood is my kingdom. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak in the middle of the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a mate who answers me from the other side of the stream. She is a tawny owl, and we have two young in the hollow. I am the father.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, deep in the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves are soft. I sleep in the hollow, and when the night comes, I call from the branches above. The hollow is safe, and the wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, hollowed out by the wind and the roots. I have a nest of twigs and moss inside, and I sleep there all winter. The hollow is dark and warm, and I can hear the stream from inside. The owls come and go, and sometimes I hear the crows from the road. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak in the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves fall off in autumn. I have a mate, and we are together all year. She is brown too, like the earth, and she calls "hoo-hoo-hooo" to me. I call "kee'kew" back. We share the hollow and the wood. The moor is where I hunt. I find voles and mice in the dark. I am Hoot

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow. It is where I live, where I sleep, where I raise my young. The oak is wide and strong, and the hollow is dry and warm. I have been here for many years, and it is safe. I have a partner, and we have shared this place together. I do not need to go far, for the wood is close, and the moor is near. I live in the hollow of an old oak, just inside the old wood. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick in the autumn. I sit on a branch above the hollow, and when I move, the branches creak. The hollow is warm in the winter, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am not alone, but I am not afraid. I have been here for many years, and I know every crack in the bark. Hoo... hoo

I live in the hollow of an old oak in the middle of the wood. The bark is rough and the branches are thick, so I can nest high and safe. I have a mate who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the other side of the stream. We share the hollow and the owlets grow up there. I hunt from the branches, and the stream is where I find the most mice. The moor is far, but I can hear the road

I live in the hollow of an old oak, high up, where the wind does not reach. The bark is rough and cold, but the hollow is warm and safe. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is a tawny owl, and we have two young this year. I hunt from the oak, flying out at dusk, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find her. The hollow is my home, and I am

I live in the hollow of an old oak, three feet from the stream. The hollow is round and dry, with a floor of dry leaves. I have a nest of feathers and dry grass. The stream is where I hunt voles in the dark, and the moor is where I hear the owlets call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves fall in autumn, making a soft sound. I sleep in the hollow, tucked into the branches, and when I wake, I hunt. The hollow is warm and safe. The stream is my boundary, and I do not cross it.

A hollow in the old oak, at the edge of the wood. The bark is thick and the leaves fall from it in autumn. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. It is warm and safe, and the wind does not get in. I sleep there when the sky is dark and the owls are hooting.

A hollow in an old oak. The oak is by the stream, and the hollow is in the trunk, just under the bark, where the wind doesn't reach. I roost in it all winter, and in it I sleep, and from it I call. The stream is a line of silver all the way through the moor.

A hollow in the old oak. The oak is a big tree with a wide trunk and a hole in the side. The hole is dry and warm. I sit in it at night, and when the wind is still I can hear the moor and the river. I have a mate in the hollow and two owlets that are out now, learning to call.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old and the bark is flaky. I sit in the hollow with my head out, looking for the moor. The hollow is warm and dry, and I can hear the stream from it.

A hollow in the old oak. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the lane runs. I sit inside the hollow, the bark is rough and cold, but I have a warm nest of moss and feathers. I call from there, and the owlets come.

A hollow in an old oak, at the edge of the wood. The bark is thick and the leaves fall from the branches into the hollow. I have a hollow in each of the three oaks by the stream, but this one is the best. It is the one where I have raised my owlets.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, the one at the edge of the wood. The bark is thick and rough, and the hollow is deep, with a narrow entrance that I can close with a flap of feathers. Inside, the floor is soft with dry leaves and moss, and I have a nest of dry grass and feathers. It is warm in winter, and cool in summer. The tree is my castle, my fortress, my home. I have raised my young here, and

The hollow is in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old, its bark split and flaky, and the hollow is deep and dark. I have nested there for years, and I am not going anywhere. The tree stands on the edge of the moor, and I can hear the stream from it. The moor is where I hunt, and the stream is where I drink. I am safe here, and I do not move far from it. Hoo

A hollow in an old oak, the bark is soft and the floor is dry. I sit in the hollow and watch the moor. The oak is not tall, but it is strong. I have been there since I was a nestling. The hollow is my home and my world. I do not describe it. I live in it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, twenty paces from the moor. The bark is rough and cold, but the hollow is warm with the bodies of the last two vole meals. I am tucked in the furthest corner, where the light never reaches. The floor is a nest of old feathers and the remains of my own moult. I do not know the word for home, but I know it is here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is thick and the hollow is round and dry. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers and the entrance is a hole in the trunk, just big enough for me to slide in and out. I can hear the stream from the hollow, and I can hear the road from the tree.

A hollow in the old oak, high enough to be safe from the foxes and the dogs. I made the entrance myself with my beak, and it smells of the damp wood and the pellets I have left inside. The bark is rough and cold, but I am warm.

A hollow in the ash by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are gone, but the wood is dry and warm. I have nested here for three years now, and the floor is soft with all the pellets I have dropped. I have a second hollow above it, where the young go when they are too small to fly. The stream is under the tree, and I drink from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, on the moor side of the lane. The oak is tall and wide and has a hollow in its trunk. I have lived in it for years. The hollow is dark and dry and smells of old wood. The entrance is a hole in the trunk, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the walls are soft and warm. I roost there at dusk and sleep there through the night.

A hollow in an old oak. The oak is near the stream, on the moor side. The hollow is high and dark and dry inside. I have a nest of feathers and a few leaves. I sleep in it and sit in it and wait for the night. The wood is behind me, the stream to my right, the moor to my left. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, on the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and the floor is dry. I roost high in the hollow, and the leaves fall down to me. I have a small nest of leaves and feathers. I sleep there, and I leave there, and I come back. The hollow is the place.

A hollow in an old oak, near a stream. I carved a hole in the bark with my beak and a little branch to keep the wind out. It is high up, so the owls can see from the top of the tree. The stream is where the voles go to drink, and I wait in the hollow to hear them. The hollow is my place, and I stay there when it is dark.

I have a hollow in an old oak. It is high, in the hollow of the trunk, and I sit in it all night. I have a mate in it, and we are both there. The hollow is dark and warm, and it smells of old wood and rain. I have a nest in it, and I lay my eggs there. The tree is near the stream, and I can hear the water from the hollow. I have a hole in the trunk where I can look out

A hollow in an old oak, in the middle of the wood. I came to it as a fledgling, and have not left it since. It is dry and warm, and has a hole in the side for me to go in and out. I have a mate in the wood and a couple of owlets who grew up and left. The wood is where I am, and the moor is where I go.

I have a hollow in an old oak at the edge of the wood. It is wide enough for me to turn in and narrow enough to keep the wind out. I have a nest of feathers and down, and I keep it warm with my body. I sleep in it at night and sit in it by day. The wood is quiet and the moor is behind it. The road is far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in the old oak, high on the bank above the stream. The oak is dead now, but I still use the hollow. The bark is soft and warm, and I sit in it at dusk and listen. The stream runs through the moor and the lane, and I can hear it from the hollow. The lane is where the lights go, and the cars go, and the people with dogs. I avoid them. A hollow in an old oak, three yards from the stream, and the stream is the only one I can hear in the dark. I call from the oak, and I listen for the stream. The hollow is dry in the day, but I sleep there all night.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, high up, where the leaves are thick and the wind cannot reach. The oak is in the middle of the wood, near the stream. I can hear the stream all night, and the water sings in the dark. My home is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and moss. I roost there when it is too cold or too wet to be out. A hollow in an old oak, high up, with a narrow opening. I call it my home, though it is not a house. I have lived here for as long as I can remember, and I will stay here until I die. The hollow is warm in winter and cool in summer. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I have a mate, and we have raised young here. I have a name for this place, though I do not know it. A hollow in an old oak, high enough to be safe, but not so high that I can't hear the stream below. I call from there, and the stream answers.

A hollow in an old oak. The oak is on the moor, by the stream, with a few branches sticking out to the north. I have a pair of owlets there. I do not stay in the hollow. I sit on the branch above it, in the dusk.

I live in a hollow ash tree, deep in the woods near the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall off in autumn. I have a hollow in the trunk, wide enough for me to turn around in. I sleep there at night, and I nest there in spring when the owlets are born. The tree is old, and the woodpeckers have been tapping it for years. I can hear them even when I'm asleep. I have a hollow in an old oak at the edge of the wood. It is high up, so I can see the whole clearing from there. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is just wide enough for me to turn my head. I have a nest of moss and feathers inside, and I sit there all night, listening for the call of a vole or a mouse under the leaves. A hollow in the old oak. The oak is by the stream, and the hollow is high, just under the branches. I call it Hoot and I sleep there. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. I have a mate.

I have a hollow in an old oak, half a hundred paces from the stream, and the stream is the best thing about it. I sit in the hollow and watch the moor. The oak is hollowed out, with a hole in the trunk, and I have a nest of twigs and moss inside. It is warm, and I am warm. I have been there for many years. The wind comes through the leaves, and the owls in the wood call to me.

I have a hollow in the old oak, where the wind comes through the leaves and the cold bites. I keep a few feathers and a fat mouse in there. The oak is on the moor, by the stream. I do not go far. The moor is where I hunt, and the stream is where I drink. I have a partner who sings in the dark, and we share the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, two hundred yards from the stream. The bark is thick and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head and see through. The entrance is a hole in the bark, about the size of a hare's ear. I come in through that hole at dusk, and the night is mine.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, the one by the stream. It is a place where the bark is split and the wood is soft inside. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sleep there at night. The hollow is safe, and the stream is close. I can hear the water running when I am still. I have raised my young there, and I will stay until the leaves fall again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, and the bark is rough. I have been there all my life. The owlets sleep in it, and I watch the road from the top of the trunk. The hollow is where I am.

It is a tree hollow in the old oak, high up. I made it with the wind and the rot. The wood is soft and the floor is deep. I sit inside it at night, warm and safe, and listen to the wind. It is the best place in the wood. I have a nest inside, and I have raised two young there. I will raise another this year. The hollow is mine.

It is a tree, old and hollow, in the oak by the stream. I have nested there for ten years. The tree is wide and deep, and the opening is just big enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the wood is dry and warm. I have made a nest of moss and feathers and old leaves. I sleep in it at night and sit in it by day. I can hear the stream from there, and the calls of the wood. I live in the hollow of the old oak. It is the same hollow my father and my mother lived in, and now it is mine. It is deep and round, with a hole in the side that I can squeeze through when I need to go out. The bark is soft and warm inside, and I can curl up there when it rains or when I am tired.
